description: We are a group of Polytechnic students. We are specialized in Coding and UX Development and UI Design Management, something which I would like to see in potential members.
summary:
Terra Analog Atlas is an interactive web atlas that helps mission planners find the best places on Earth to rehearse for the Moon and Mars.

Our challenge asks teams to identify and characterise terrestrial analogs for lunar and Martian bases and landing sites. We gathered 15 Earth sites, from the Atacama Desert to Antarctica’s McMurdo Dry Valleys, and scored each on eight factors: geology, terrain, temperature, water and ice, dust and wind, habitability, caves and subsurface, and landing operations. Users pick one of 20 real destinations, such as the Mare Tranquillitatis pit on the Moon or Jezero Crater on Mars. The atlas ranks the Earth sites by how closely they match, shows them on a satellite map, and adds climate figures from NASA POWER.

Crews, rovers and habitats must be tested on Earth first. The atlas makes it quicker to choose the right test site for each mission, and makes clear what that site cannot simulate.
details:
What it does and how it works
Terra Analog Atlas is a website with three pages.

Atlas: you choose the Moon or Mars, then one of 20 real destination sites, 10 on each. The atlas ranks 15 Earth sites by how well they match that destination and shows them on a satellite map. You can filter by terrain, such as desert, polar, volcanic or lava tube. Clicking a site flies the map to it and opens a panel with its scores, why it matches, where the comparison breaks down, which field campaigns have used it, and climate figures from NASA POWER.

Ranking: one table compares every Earth site on all eight factors.

Challenge: this page explains the scoring, the Moon and Mars conditions we are matching, and our data sources and references.

Each Earth site has a score from 0 to 100 on eight factors. Each destination weighs those factors differently: a lunar lava-tube pit puts the most weight on caves and subsurface, and a flat Mars landing plain puts the most on terrain. The match score is the weighted average, so the same Earth site can lead for one destination and drop down for another.

For the four lunar south-pole sites, we exported terrain and hydrogen data from LROC QuickMap and processed it with a Python script. The other Moon sites and the Mars sites are described from published papers.

Key features and benefits

  • Rankings that change with the destination, across 20 Moon and Mars sites.
  • A satellite map that flies to each Earth site.
  • Climate figures for every Earth site, read live from NASA POWER.
  • A side-by-side table of all sites and factors.
  • Every site lists what it cannot simulate, such as low gravity or vacuum.
  • Animated planets, an astronaut guide and terrain icons make it friendly for students as well as researchers.

It turns a long literature search into a few clicks, and it runs in any modern browser.

Technologies and tools

  • Website: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, Framer Motion, Radix UI and Lucide icons.
  • Map: Leaflet and React Leaflet with Esri World Imagery.
  • Server: a small Node.js and Express server written in TypeScript, which serves the built site.
  • Data: the NASA POWER API, and LROC QuickMap exports processed with Python.
  • Build: a PowerShell script (build.ps1) using npm or pnpm.
  • Other: GitHub. AI tools: Base44 for the first version of the site, and Claude for the graphics and the animation, sound and map code (labelled on the site).

    How to run it
    Install Node.js, clone our repository, and run build.ps1 in the cloned folder. Then open http://localhost:3000 in a browser.
